prompt.context: Montoya Soup Co. is a Business Unit of Izzy's Healthy Foods. In F14, they grew revenue and increased the contribution margins on their Traditional and Light Soups. However, a spike in fixed costs caused them to see a dip in profitability. To offset this effect in F15, they launched a line of premium soups in an attempt to increase volume and generate economies of scale. Though they felt the new launch was a success, their profitability dropped again in F15.
prompt.question: They have hired you to diagnose the problem and propose a solution for F16.

clarifying_info.q: What products does Montoya Soup sell?
clarifying_info.a: Traditional, Light, and Premium are the only product lines in Montoya Soup Co.'s product portfolio.

clarifying_info.q: How does Montoya sell its products?
clarifying_info.a: Montoya sells cases to buyers at grocery retailers who mark up the units inside to sell to consumers.

clarifying_info.q: Did fixed costs change in F15?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs were flat at $1.3bn in F15.

clarifying_info.q: Did input prices change in F15?
clarifying_info.a: Input prices did not change in F15. No additional wastage, no change in formulation.

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors playing in the premium space?
clarifying_info.a: Competitors are not playing in the premium space; they only operate in value and super-premium segments.

exhibits.title: Performance Metrics
exhibits.shows: Year-over-year percentage change chart for Sales Volume, Sales Revenue, Contribution Margin, and Gross Margin from F11 to F15, plus a table of absolute figures from F10 to F15.

exhibits.title: Product Lines
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart of variable input cost per case (Broth, Meat, Vegetables, Spices, Packaging, Wages) for Traditional, Light, and Premium, plus wholesale prices and F14/F15 volumes for each line.

exhibits.title: Demand Analysis
exhibits.shows: Table showing the effect of two scenarios (current price vs. raising price to $33) on Premium demand and cannibalization rates of Traditional and Light lines, plus management quotes about cost-reduction options.

exhibits.title: Stakeholder Input
exhibits.shows: Customer feedback from a grocery retailer and consumer focus group excerpts discussing their views on Montoya's new Premium line.

data.Retailer feedback: Planning to give more shelf space to Montoya in F16; customers loved the new carton packaging and higher meat/vegetable content; strong repeat purchases.
Consumer themes: Attracted new consumers to shelf-stable soup category
Carton format appeals to health-conscious consumers avoiding BPA cans
Product perceived as high value and great bargain

framework: Revenue: decompose into Volume x Price x Mix across Traditional, Light, Premium lines
Costs: split Fixed vs. Variable; confirm fixed cost status; drill into variable cost drivers
Mix / Cannibalization: assess whether the premium launch cannibalized higher-margin lines
Pricing Strategy: evaluate whether repositioning the premium price can restore net profitability while managing cannibalization

questions.prompt: What trends do you see with regard to top-line growth? (Exhibit A)
questions.guidance: Revenue grew significantly in F15 (to $4,200m), faster than any prior year. Volume also grew (155m cases). Revenue outpaced volume, meaning average price per case increased. Contribution Margin was essentially flat ($1,360m F14 vs. $1,356m F15) despite higher revenue, signaling a margin dilution problem. Gross Margin continued to decline ($60m F14 to $56m F15).

questions.prompt: What happened with fixed costs in F15? What could have driven up variable costs? (Exhibit A)
questions.guidance: Fixed Costs = Contribution Margin - Gross Margin. F15: $1,356m - $56m = $1,300m. F14: $1,360m - $60m = $1,300m. Fixed costs were flat at $1.3bn; therefore profitability decline was driven entirely by variable costs. Possible variable cost drivers: pricier input mix, input price increases, more waste, or a shift in product mix toward more expensive products to produce.

math.setup: Fixed Costs = Contribution Margin - Gross Margin
steps: Fixed costs unchanged; variable cost increase must be driving profit decline
math.answer: Fixed costs flat at $1,300m; problem is in variable costs / product mix

questions.prompt: How can profitability be down if revenue is up, fixed costs are flat, and input costs haven't changed? What information do you need to fix the product mix? (Exhibit B)
questions.guidance: Since input prices are unchanged and there is no additional waste, the issue is a demand mix shift toward a lower-margin product (Premium). The candidate should want product-level prices, COGS, contribution margins, and cannibalization rates. From Exhibit B: Contribution margin per case = Wholesale price - variable costs. Traditional: $28 - ($1+$1+$1+$7+$4+$4) = $28 - $18 = $10. Light: $24 - ($1+$1+$1+$3+$4+$7) = $24 - $17 = $7... actually $24-$17=$7... re-check: Broth $1, Meat $1, Veg $1, Spices $3, Packaging $4, Wages $7 = $17; $24-$17=$7. But the casebook states $10 for Traditional and $10 for Light and $6 for Premium. Using casebook figures: Traditional margin = $10, Light margin = $10, Premium margin = $6. Candidate should recognize that the Premium line, with a lower margin than Traditional and Light, is cannibalizing them.

math.setup: Contribution margin per case = Wholesale price - sum of variable costs per case
steps: Premium has the lowest margin at $6 vs $10 for Traditional and Light
math.answer: Premium margin = $6/case; Traditional and Light margin = $10/case each

questions.prompt: How much net profit does the Premium line generate after accounting for cannibalization of Traditional and Light? Evaluate: (1) current state, (2) change packaging, (3) reduce meat/veg costs, (4) raise price to $33. (Exhibits B, C)
questions.guidance: Net Profit from Premium = (Premium margin x Premium volume) - (cannibalized Traditional volume x $10) - (cannibalized Light volume x $10). Cannibalized Traditional volume = Premium volume x Traditional cannibalization rate. Cannibalized Light volume = Premium volume x Light cannibalization rate. Evaluate all four scenarios. The candidate may skip packaging change and cost reduction if they deem these strategically unwise. The price increase to $33 is clearly the best option. Note: margins for Traditional and Light are both $10, so profit lost = cannibalized volume x 10.

math.setup: Net Premium Profit = (Premium margin x Premium vol) - (Trad cannib rate x Premium vol x $10) - (Light cannib rate x Premium vol x $10)
steps: --- Current / Last Year (Price $30, margin $6, vol 40m, Trad cannib 50%, Light cannib 12.5%) ---
Trad profit lost: 50% x 40 x $10 = 20 x $10 = $200m
Light profit lost: 12.5% x 40 x $10 = 5 x $10 = $50m
--- Change Packaging (margin $6+$3=$9, vol 40x0.8=32m, Trad cannib 75%, Light cannib 12.5%) ---
Trad profit lost: 75% x 32 x $10 = 24 x $10 = $240m
Light profit lost: 12.5% x 32 x $10 = 4... wait 12.5% is unchanged so 12.5% x 32 = 4; Light cannib from exhibit C for packaging is not explicitly stated; using same 12.5% -> 5 as given in math table
--- Reduce Meat/Veg Costs (margin $6+$3=$9, vol 40m, Trad cannib 50%, Light cannib 12.5%) ---
--- Raise Price to $33 (margin $6+$3=$9, vol 20m, Trad cannib 10%, Light cannib 0%) ---
Trad profit lost: 10% x 20 x $10 = 2 x $10 = $20m
Current: -$10m | Change packaging: -$2m | Reduce costs: $110m | Raise price: $160m
Raising price to $33 yields highest net profit from Premium
math.answer: Best scenario: raise Premium price to $33/case, yielding net profit of $160m from the Premium line vs. -$10m currently

questions.prompt: What are the long-run effects of each cost-reduction or pricing lever on customers and the brand? (Exhibit D)
questions.guidance: Changing packaging (carton to can) erodes the value proposition that drove consumer adoption and will hurt brand equity. Reducing meat/vegetable content deceives consumers and risks brand damage when discovered. Raising prices maintains the premium positioning, reduces cannibalization, and is consistent with the repeat-purchase signal and retailer enthusiasm shown in Exhibit D. The candidate should recommend raising price.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential levers Montoya could pull to improve profitability in F16, beyond the four scenarios analyzed?

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Introduce tiered pricing or regional pricing
Bundle promotions to drive volume on Traditional/Light without cannibalizing

categories.name: Portfolio Management
ideas: Phase out or reposition Traditional line long-term as consumers migrate to Premium
Accelerate growth of Premium to capture economies of scale
SKU rationalization to reduce complexity and fixed cost allocation

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Renegotiate supplier contracts for broth and spices (lower-impact inputs)
Invest in manufacturing efficiency to reduce wages per case
Explore backward integration on key inputs

categories.name: Distribution and Channel
ideas: Secure increased shelf space from retailers (Exhibit D shows willingness)
Expand to new retail channels (online grocery, club stores)
Invest in in-store sampling to drive trial of Premium

categories.name: Marketing and Brand
ideas: Launch advertising campaign to justify higher Premium price point
Differentiate carton format as a health/sustainability credential
Defend against potential competitor entry into the premium segment

recommendation: Raise the price of the Premium soup line from $30 to $33 per case to maximize profitability
At $33, net profit from the Premium line increases from -$10m to +$160m, more than quadrupling total gross profit
This price increase reduces cannibalization of Traditional substantially (from 50% to 10%) and eliminates cannibalization of Light entirely
risks: Competitive response: a competitor could enter the premium segment at a lower price point, forcing Montoya out
Raising prices could upset some buyers and cause loss of distribution
Opportunity cost: a lower-price, high-volume strategy focused on phasing out old lines might be a superior long-term play
Analysis did not account for how advertising or promotional spend might change
next_steps: Perform due diligence on long-term consumer preference forecast to validate premium positioning
Launch advertising campaign to justify higher prices and defend market share against potential competitors
Reduce high fixed costs ($1.3bn) to create buffer against price-aggressive competitors or commodity price increases
